question: What are the two main parts the human body is divided into?
explanation: Think of the body in two parts: the central core (axial) and the limbs attached to it (appendicular). Easy peasy! [learn more](GNS111_U1_T4#GNS111_U1_T4_h1)

question: Why do nurses use standard body terms in patient charts?

options.A: To ensure the patient cannot read or understand their chart
options.B: To fulfill strict legal requirements set by pharmaceutical companies
options.C: To make patient records look more professional and complex
options.D: To prevent misunderstandings among healthcare team members

explanation: Using the same medical language ensures every nurse and doctor instantly understands exactly where a patient is feeling pain or injury. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T4#GNS111_U1_T4_h1)

question: Which of these body areas is part of the axial region?
explanation: The axial region covers your head, neck, and trunk—the main central pillar of your body! [learn more](GNS111_U1_T4#GNS111_U1_T4_h2)

question: What is a main job of the trunk in the axial skeleton?
explanation: Your chest and belly trunk acts like a strong shield for your heart, lungs, and tummy organs. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T4#GNS111_U1_T4_h2)

question: Which of these belongs to the appendicular region?
explanation: Your arms and legs (limbs) make up the appendicular region. Think of them as the appendages attached to your main body! [learn more](GNS111_U1_T4#GNS111_U1_T4_h3)

question: A patient falls and breaks their thigh bone (femur). Which body region is hurt?
explanation: Since the femur is in the leg, it belongs to the appendicular region. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T4#GNS111_U1_T4_h3)

question: Into how many standard sections (quadrants) do we map the tummy area?
explanation: We easily map out the abdomen using four quadrants: right upper, left upper, right lower, and left lower. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T4#GNS111_U1_T4_h4)

question: Why do nurses use the four-quadrant system during a quick tummy check?

options.A: To calculate the exact body mass index of the patient
options.B: To measure the respiratory rate and lung capacity
options.C: To easily localize pain and internal organ locations
options.D: To determine the correct dosage of oral medications

explanation: Dividing the tummy into four helps you quickly guess which organ might be troubling your patient. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T4#GNS111_U1_T4_h4)

question: Which of these is found on the front (anterior) part of the body?
explanation: Your umbilicus is your belly button—right there on the front of your body! [learn more](GNS111_U1_T4#GNS111_U1_T4_h5)

question: You need to listen to a patient's breathing from their back. Which landmarks will guide you?
explanation: The shoulder blade (scapula) and spine (vertebral column) are great back landmarks for placing your stethoscope. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T4#GNS111_U1_T4_h5)

question: What is the danger of writing vague notes like 'stomach pain' in a patient's chart?

options.A: It prevents the patient from receiving any pain medication
options.B: It causes the hospital electronic health record system to crash
options.C: It can lead to miscommunication and delayed treatment among staff
options.D: It automatically invalidates the nurse's nursing license

explanation: Vague notes leave other nurses guessing, which can slow down proper care. Always aim for clear, specific charting! [learn more](GNS111_U1_T4#GNS111_U1_T4_h6)

question: Which chart note shows the best use of proper anatomical descriptions?

options.A: Ouch in the leg area when the nurse touches the skin
options.B: Patient is complaining of general body pain everywhere
options.C: Tenderness noted in the left upper quadrant during palpation
options.D: Sore spot on the middle part of the body trunk

explanation: Spot on! Using specific terms like 'left upper quadrant' gives your team exact, helpful clinical details. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T4#GNS111_U1_T4_h6)
